photo.title: A friend of informant Deborah, Naomi Tudrinwa, is firing her pots, a continuation of 2008.78.175 and 210 onwards. Images of pottery-making can be seen between 2008.78.2.90-101 and in 2008.78.2.150 Naomi herself is making a pot. Naomi has friends to help her fire the pots. They have prepared the firing materials between three tree trunks, and in this image pots are seen between smouldering logs, and a friend looks stands nearby. They had placed bark and sticks over the ground, put the pots among them and cover the pots with more stick to fire them.  Patti Langton [30/06/2009]

Lui Junior Secondary School written in English and Arabic outside the school compound. Two huts and a building can be seen in the distance. The school was built in 1975 by the Sudan Council of Churches. The first school was opened in Lui by Dr, Frazer, a missionary, who brought Christianity to the area in the 1920's, built a church, a school and a hospital in the area, and brought peace as well. Between 1965-72, during the civil war, the Moru Misa people scattered into the hills, and were only just settling back again when we visited. Some still hadn't returned. Patti Langton [28/07/2009]

Lui Junior Secondary School written in English and Arabic outside the school compound. Two huts and a building can be seen in the distance. The school was built in 1975 by the Sudan Council of Churches. The first school was opened in Lui by Dr, Frazer, a missionary, who brought Christianity to the area in the 1920's, built a church, a school and a hospital in the area, and brought peace as well. Between 1965-72, during the civil war, the Moru Misa people scattered into the hills, and were only just settling back again when we visited. Some still hadn't returned. Patti Langton [28/07/2009]

The campsite of the expedition at Lui village. The tents are in a semi-circle and John Mack, the other anthropologist on the expedition, sits working at a table in the corner. Patti Langton [09/11/2010]

Women stay in a special birthing hut to have their babies. Deborah, the main informant,  constructed this hut for her daughter. The hut entrance faces north. After the birth a shelter of grasses is put round the hut. If the baby is a girl they stay for 4 days afterwards, 3 days if it is a boy. Traditionally the boy would be wrapped in special bark cloth. Today all babies are wrapped in cotton. (See 2008.78.1.1) Patti Langton [16/11/2010]
Naomi Tudrinwa, potter, is firing her pots. Deborah helps to the right of frame. [Patti Langton [23/11/2010]
A lovely cool river where members of the expedition could go in the early evening to swim. Patti Langton [23/11/2010]

Decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.  A village can be seen behind. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid them. Co-worker Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound. Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has three 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. (See also 2008.78.1.41). One of the expedition landrovers can be seen in the background. Patti Langton [23/11/2010]

An old DIRI drum sits on the ground, images of footprints all around. The DIRI drum is a special form of  medium sized drum, used solely for funerals. When someone died they used to beat the drum. It is made of WERE wood, with a pigskin (wild boar) cover and hide fronds which are plaited around it. In Deborah's (informant) compound. Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

An image of a gourd used as a dance rattle, GARA. It is placed on the ground to be photographed  in informant Deborah's compound. It is hollowed out and filed with sorghum seeds, and cassava leaves stuffed in the neck. The traditional rattle dance, still enacted from 9pm to morning, for ceremonies. Women use the rattles and dance in the inner circle, while the men, without rattles, dance in the outer circle the opposite way. These days the rattles are also used in Church, and at dances on Friday night. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

This is a side view of a winnowing tray, KUBI, made with DURA fronds from the stem of the sorghum (durrha) plant. Small fronds make an intricate weave, with coloured fronds interwoven. In Deborah's (informant) compound. Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

A top view of a meat pot, MOLA, sits on the ground in Deborah (informant's) compound. This is a medium sized meat pot. It has a plain rim and cross-hatched body. MOLA is the correct name (not Moya as in the primary documentation) Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

An image of the cooking hearth in Deborah's (informant) compound. Two fires stones can be seen round the hearth, with a nearly burned branch, and the third fire stone sitting a little was to the right. A hollow log sits by the hearth, maybe to rest bellows. The shadow of the anthropologist taking the photograph is clearly seen to the left of frame. Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

Hut belonging to Deborah's (informant) mother. The exterior mud has been washed off and not replaced leaving the skeleton exposed. As an elderly widow, it is likely she will have to wait for a younger family member to help her to repair the hut. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

In this image, informant Deborah's mother stands in front of her sleeping hut, ZO. The exterior mud has been washed off and not replaced leaving the skeleton exposed. As an elderly widow, it is likely she will have to wait for a younger family member to help her to repair the hut. Deborah's mother has a number of houses to tend, as she has children living in Juba and Maridi. They have their village house also. To the right of the mother's sleeping hut, a hut is hidden by a high fence. This is where Deborah's daughter recently gave birth. The baby is now 3 weeks old. The reason given for the fence was to "prevent wind affecting the birth". Birth is followed by 4-7 days' seclusion. A bed of logs is located to the right of Deborah's mother's hut and a large pot, LUKUDU, sits in the centre of the compound (probably to be photographed). Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

A wooden stirrer for stirring porridge, BARI. It is placed on the ground for photographing. Porridge is the non-fermented form, which, when fermented becomes 'beer'. Porridge can be made from ground sorghum (durrha), sesame (simsim) and groundnuts. Sorghum alone is quite sour, sesame sweetens it. A light porridge Deborah compared with tea - "it warms your blood." Porridge has a smooth consistency, and can be thick or quite liquid. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]
This stone 'house' is the chicken hut. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

In the informant Deborah's compound there is an area for graves. They are set in a circle, each one different. Deborah had 6 sisters and 3 brothers. 3 sisters died as babies, and at least one as an adult. This grave belongs to an aunt.  The megalith faces west as she was female. The stones are piled to a height of about 100cm and the megalith is 199cm high. You can see the outline of the triangular heap of stones denoting a leper's grave directly behind.  Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

In this image informant Deborah stands to the side of her father's grave, which is a mixture of Christian and traditional, with the tall vertical megalith on a Christian-style base. He was a chief. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

A young girl sits on a mat, in front of the entrance to her hut making pottery coils, BIRI BIRI. In front of her is the beginning of a pot, about five coils are already built up on top of an old pottery base, KAGYE,  which is used to create the shape. The girl is adding a coil to the pot. She keeps it moist with water in a metal pot beside her. There is a sequence of this pot being made, unfortunately I've not quite filed it in the right order, but you can see where it goes wrong by the number of coils! The long stick beside her is her walking stick, she had polio as a young child.  (See 2008.78.2.90-101; also 2008.78.1.12). Patti Langton [30/03/2009]

A  side view of a trap, on Jebel Tikye, the tree trunk clearly visible. Small animals, including gazelle and baboon would be caught in these. (See 2008.78.2.96-119, also 2008.78.1.28-35). Patti Langton [11/05/2009]

This is a Mangaviri trap for capturing small animals like gazelle. There is a tree trunk bent over sticks. A noose is hanging from it down to almost ground level. In this trap vegetation has been woven round the trap to hide it. The animal catches its foot in the noose, the tree bends back and the animal is caught.  (See 2008.78.2.96-119, also 2008.78.1.28-35). Patti Langton [11/05/2009]

A Moru grave, one of a cluster. It is round, with a flat slab on top. This will have been an elder's grave. Patti Langton [11/05/2009]

A young girl sits on the ground, weaving  basket. The fronds (DIRI) are made from the  DURA plant. The basket-maker makes a small square basket base as in the image. She will then then take an old basket, and thread the DIRI fronds of the new base through. The new basket is woven over the old basket for a few centimetres to get the shape, after which she'll detach the old basket and continue to make the new one (see also photos between 2008.78.2.147-157). Patti Langton [19/05/2009]

The Lui village shop is a rectangular building with a corrugated iron door and roof.  The shopkeeper stands in front with his three children. In the background there are two hut skeletons, one possibly old and the other waiting for its covering with mud and thatch. Next door are two older huts with traditional thatching. [Patti Langton 02/03/2009]
A group of children sit in front of a round hut in the compound of one of the interpreters, Andrea. [Patti Langton 02/03/2009]

A woman enters her hut through a corrugated door. The entrance faces west, indicating it is a woman's hut. Another hut stands nearby. Both have traditional low thatch roofs. The  compound belongs to an interpreter, Andrea. [Patti Langton 02/03/2009]

An image of the new house built by interpreter Andrea in his compound. It isn't quite finished, the thatched roof is not quite done. It is a large rectangular house, quite different from traditional round huts. Andrea is very proud of his house. Patti Langton [12/07/2011]

In the foreground two young women sit, one plaits the hair of the other. Both wear 'Western style' dresses, showing the influence of Christianity in this part of Moru.  In the background, a young girl watches, and another woman tends her baby. Patti Langton [12/07/2011]
